title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 15: Postscript to A Centenary of Justice
keywords: Postscript to A Centenary of Justice
Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's postscript reporting the readers' response to 'A Centenary of Justice,' the fifth book he had written since joining the Supreme Court in 1995, and using that response to explain why he publishes a book every year.

His account of the annual book as an instrument of public accountability and transparency -- a jurist's yearly report on his own work, so that the public may be certain he acted conscientiously, 'letting only truth, the law, reason and my conscience dictate my actions.'

His description of the books as a 'window to the Court,' recounting how the justices argued, deliberated, voted and decided landmark and controversial cases, illustrated by the SWS survey-ban case and by Perez v. Estrada, in which he dissented.

His reporting of the book's reception -- nearly a hundred letters from magistrates at home and abroad, officials, educators, churchmen and librarians, plus newspaper columns and broadcast mentions -- as evidence of a growing public demand for transparency in government and in institutions that bear on the public weal.
sub_topics: He reports being overwhelmed by close to a hundred letters of felicitation on 'A Centenary of Justice,' from judiciary members, foreign Chief Justices and magistrates, executive officials, legislators, diplomats, educators, church and lay leaders, lawyers, NGO leaders and librarians.
He is especially elated that President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo found time to write, and notes that former President Fidel V. Ramos's letter is unique because it is entirely handwritten.

He singles out the letter of Brother Willy Nakar of Elim, who found it edifying that 'a man of the law' should begin his books with the Word of God, and admits surprise that anyone noticed that regular feature.

He thanks the newspapermen and women who cited or reviewed the book in their columns and the television and radio commentators who mentioned it, saying he has noted their comments and suggestions for future books.

He explains the origin of the annual book in 1995, when he was sworn into the highest court and recognized that, like all government servants, he is accountable to the public and should adhere to transparency in the performance of his duties.

He lists the series that followed that commitment: 'Justice and Faith' (1997), 'Battles in the Supreme Court' (1998), 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' (1999), 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000), 'A Centenary of Justice' (2001) and the present 'Reforming the Judiciary' (2002), which he hopes to continue until retirement.

He notes that the Supreme Court Press publishes the books in limited press runs, distributing them to government offices, libraries, law schools, NGOs and media, and that organizations and individuals write asking for copies -- sometimes of all five -- although the books 'can hardly be described as literary potboilers.'

He attributes the demand to society's growing awareness of the need for transparency, quoting CHED Chairperson Ester Albano Garcia's March 4, 2002 letter that public education about the Court's constitutional task 'can only be helpful to the Supreme Court -- and to the judiciary as a whole.'

He ties accountability and transparency to the Court's judicial reform program, cites readers' encouragement for the 'monumental task' being undertaken with Chief Justice Davide, and explains that this is why the present book concentrates on the 'Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006.'
He describes the window-to-the-Court function of his books: discussing controversial and landmark cases that caused diversity in the opinions and legal philosophies of the members of the Court.

He recounts that his chapter on Social Weather Stations v. Comelec became the subject of Dr. Mahar Mangahas's January 7, 2001 Manila Standard column 'The Right to Be Subjective,' which thanked him for the earlier exit-polling decision and for helping teach lawyers and laymen about freedom of speech.

He recounts the chapter on Perez v. Estrada, the 8-6 denial of Secretary of Justice Hernando Perez's request for live radio and television coverage of Joseph Ejercito Estrada's Sandiganbayan plunder trial, in which Justice Jose C. Vitug's decision held that the right of the accused 'must be preferred.'

He recalls his own Dissent arguing that ten years after the 1991 ban it was already technologically possible to uphold the people's right to information without violating the accused's right to due process, and quotes Beth Day Romulo's Manila Bulletin column reporting his view that the Court was 'turning its back' on modern technology and the people's right to know.
He relays readers' descriptions of the experience as 'being privy to ponencias and separate opinions' and as offering outsiders deeper insight into the workings of the Court.

He explains that 'A Centenary of Justice' was above all about the Supreme Court's centennial, which he served as chair of the Centenary Executive Committee, devoting the book's first twelve chapters to the more than 50 activities and projects the Execom spearheaded.

He shares the letter of Justice Dorit Beinisch of the Supreme Court of Israel, who reserved a shelf for his books, cherished her participation in the centenary celebrations, and quoted back his own line that law is territorial in scope but its basic principles on human rights and civil liberties are universal.
He closes by thanking those who reserved shelf space for his books and the media men and women whose reviews and critiques have guided him from one book to the next.

notable_anecdotes: The handwritten letter: among close to a hundred letters of congratulation, he singles out former President Fidel V. Ramos's as unique because it was written entirely by hand.

Noticed at last: Brother Willy Nakar of Elim wrote that it was edifying to see a man of the law begin his books with the Word of God, and CJP admits he was pleasantly surprised anyone noticed that recurring feature.
Requests for all five: he reports the surprise and delight of organizations and individuals writing to ask for copies, sometimes of all five books, though they are no leisure reading.

A shelf in Jerusalem: Justice Dorit Beinisch of the Supreme Court of Israel wrote that she had reserved a special shelf for his books and was waiting for the next one, recalling her visit to the centenary celebrations.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' was CJP's postscript to his previous book, 'A Centenary of Justice.' He reported being overwhelmed by close to a hundred congratulatory letters from members of the judiciary, foreign Chief Justices and magistrates, officials, legislators, diplomats, educators, churchmen, lawyers, NGO leaders and librarians, singling out a letter from President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and an entirely handwritten one from former President Fidel V. Ramos, as well as Brother Willy Nakar's note praising his habit of beginning each book with the Word of God. He explained the practice behind the books: since being sworn into the Supreme Court in 1995 he had recognized that, like all government servants, he was accountable to the public and should adhere to transparency, owing readers the certainty that he had worked conscientiously, 'letting only truth, the law, reason and my conscience dictate my actions.' He listed the resulting series from 'Justice and Faith' in 1997 through the present volume, noted that the Supreme Court Press issued them in limited runs for libraries, law schools, NGOs and media, and observed with amusement that people wrote asking for all five even though the books were no 'literary potboilers.' He attributed the demand to a wider public appetite for transparency, quoting CHED Chairperson Ester Albano Garcia, and linked it to the Court's reform program under Chief Justice Davide, which is why the present book concentrated on the Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006. He then described the books as a 'window to the Court,' citing Mahar Mangahas's Manila Standard column on his chapter about the SWS survey-ban case and his chapter on Perez v. Estrada, where the Court denied live coverage of the Estrada plunder trial 8-6 and he dissented, arguing it was already technologically possible to serve the people's right to information without violating the accused's due process -- a view Beth Day Romulo relayed in the Manila Bulletin as the Court 'turning its back' on technology. He closed with his chairmanship of the Centenary Executive Committee, a letter from Justice Dorit Beinisch of Israel's Supreme Court, and thanks to his readers and reviewers.
